rows.speaker: Sh, W
rows.claim: Some commentators regard this as one of the Qur’an’s most difficult verses.
rows.anchor: Some commentators consider this verse to be among the most difficult verses of the Quran

rows.speaker: Bḍ, IK, Q, Sh
rows.claim: Most commentators say the disbelievers among the People of the Book include both Jews and Christians.
rows.anchor: According to most commentators, those who disbelieve among the People of the Book refers to disbelievers among both Jews and Christians

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A minority identifies the People of the Book here only as the Jews of Medina.
rows.anchor: though some say it refers only to the Jews of Madinah

rows.speaker: Q, R, Sh, Z
rows.claim: The majority understand the verse to mean that disbelievers persist in disbelief until revelation’s clear proof arrives.
rows.anchor: Most read this verse to mean that disbelievers will not leave their disbelief until the clear proof of revelation has come to them

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: Another reading is that people will not be punished or destroyed before revelation brings them proof; the idolaters are not abandoned but tested by their response.
rows.anchor: they will not be punished or destroyed until the proof of revelation has been brought to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading fits the principle that God sends truth through a messenger before punishing people for wrong belief and may concern rejection of Muhammad’s prophethood rather than God’s existence.
rows.anchor: God will not punish any for wrong belief until they have been presented with the truth and then rejected it

rows.speaker: Q, R, Sh
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the clear proof as the Quran.
rows.anchor: Most interpret the clear proof as a reference to the Quran

rows.speaker: Q, R, Sh
rows.claim: Others identify the clear proof as the Prophet Muhammad.
rows.anchor: Others take clear proof as a reference to the Prophet Muhammad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proof can mean revelation, books, and prophets sent to every community, since the Quran uses this expression for many prophets and their scriptures.
rows.anchor: a reference to the phenomena of revelation and thus to the books and prophets sent to all communities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this reading, the People of the Book are those said to have altered scriptures sent through earlier prophets.
rows.anchor: those who are said to have altered the scriptures that had been sent to them through previous prophets

rows.speaker: Bg, IK, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Most commentators take the purified scriptures as the Quran and the messenger as Muhammad.
rows.anchor: The majority of commentators interpret scriptures purified as a reference to the Quran and a messenger as a reference to Muhammad

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: The messenger may instead be Gabriel.
rows.anchor: Messenger can, however, also be read as a reference to the Archangel Gabriel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both terms may refer more generally to the messengers and revelations sent to every community, each of which had a warner.
rows.anchor: both terms could be seen as references to the messengers and revelations that each community has been sent

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: The purified scriptures may refer to the Preserved Tablet, from which revelation descends.
rows.anchor: Scriptures purified can also be read as a reference to the Preserved Tablet

rows.speaker: IK, Sh
rows.claim: Upright books are error-free because they come from God.
rows.anchor: Books upright indicates that they are free from errors and mistakes because they are from God

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: They distinguish truth from falsehood and contain no crookedness.
rows.anchor: distinguishing between truth and falsehood with no crookedness therein

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Their pages are honored, exalted, and purified.
rows.anchor: they are on pages honored, exalted and purified

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse echoes the pattern that communities divide after receiving knowledge and clear proofs; 3:105 warns believers against repeating it.
rows.anchor: they differed not till after knowledge had come unto them, out of envy among themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view says people were united in disbelief, then divided after revelation’s proof as some believed and others rejected it.
rows.anchor: people had been unified in their disbelief, but that after the clear proofs of revelation came, they differed

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another view says some People of the Book expected a messenger but rejected Muhammad when he arrived, despite recognizing the confirming Book.
rows.anchor: those among the People of the Book who believed that a messenger would come

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that earlier communities corrupted pure revelation, argued, and split into sects.
rows.anchor: a reference to the corruption of pure revelation by previous religious communities

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith says Jews split into 71 sects, Christians into 72, and this community into 73, with one saved group following the Prophet and his Companions.
rows.anchor: The Prophet was then asked, “Who are they, O Messenger of God?”

rows.speaker: Sh, Z
rows.claim: The opening phrase means earlier communities were commanded only to do what was enjoined for worshiping God.
rows.anchor: those who came before were only ordered to do that which was enjoined upon them in order to worship God

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: This wording implies that they mixed other practices and beliefs into the pure religion sent by God.
rows.anchor: they sought other objectives and mixed other practices and beliefs into the pure religion that God had sent them

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: Mukhlis means making something pure with complete sincerity, both in religious practice and understanding and in oneself.
rows.anchor: making something pure and doing something with complete sincerity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanīf derives from ‘incline’ and denotes turning away from idolatry toward God’s Oneness; Abraham and the Prophet are described or commanded this way.
rows.anchor: meaning “to incline.” It is employed in the Quran to indicate one who inclines away from idolatry and toward belief in the Oneness of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakāh names mandatory Muslim alms but is also used for alms among earlier communities and for charity generally.
rows.anchor: the technical term for the Muslim mandatory alms

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root of zakāh means purification: giving purifies both a person and their wealth; here it may encompass kindness to the poor, especially if the surah predates formal alms.
rows.anchor: The root meaning of zakāh is purification, implying that giving wealth purifies both the giver and the wealth

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: In this context zakāh may broadly mean every act of kindness toward poor and needy people.
rows.anchor: zakāh can be more broadly conceived as all acts of kindness toward the poor and needy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The upright religion is variously taken as Abraham’s religion, Muhammad’s specific message, or more generally the revealed way followed through a prophet.
rows.anchor: The upright religion is seen by some as a reference to the religion of Abraham and his followers

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Some specifically identify the upright religion with the religion brought by Muhammad.
rows.anchor: others see it as a more general reference to all those who follow what has been revealed to them through a prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity’s capacity to be both best and worst of creation shows its unique cosmic station: honored and favored when fulfilling its potential, but lower than animals when it fails.
rows.anchor: That human beings can be both the best of creation and the worst of creation testifies to their unique place in the cosmos

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The descriptions may mean the worst and best people of their respective ages.
rows.anchor: those who are the worst or the best of the age in which they live

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: In Sunni and Shiite reports, the Prophet told ʿAlī that he and his partisans would be the best of creation at the Resurrection, content and contenting.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib regarding the best of creation

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The combination of being best of creation and mutual contentment indicates humanity’s illustrious station.
rows.anchor: The combination of the best of creation and the mutual contentment mentioned in v. 8 indicates that human beings have an illustrious station

rows.speaker: Āl, IK
rows.claim: Some scholars infer that believing, righteous humans are better than angels.
rows.anchor: believing and righteous human beings are better than the angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others take the phrase to mean believers are the best among created beings in this world.
rows.anchor: believers as the best among the created beings in this world

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet called a fighter defending God’s way and a shepherd who prays and gives alms among the best of creation, and one who refuses a God-directed request among the worst.
rows.anchor: He replied, “A man who takes the reins of his horse in the way of God

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Another hadith says a believer is more noble in God’s sight than some angels.
rows.anchor: The believer is more noble in the Eyes of God than some of His angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the Garden of Contentment is Paradise’s second-highest level, below the Garden of the Essence.
rows.anchor: the second highest level of Paradise, just below the Garden of the Essence

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: The surah is dated either late in the Meccan period or to Medina in 623, shortly after the Hijrah, and is named for the earth’s shaking.
rows.anchor: either a late Makkan sūrah or a Madinan sūrah revealed in 623

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first five verses describe the earthquake as a Judgment event; the final three describe the weighing of good and evil deeds.
rows.anchor: The first five verses provide a powerful and extended discussion of the quaking of the earth

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet directed a man who struggled with longer recitations to recite al-Zalzalah; the man vowed to recite only it, and the Prophet said he had prospered.
rows.anchor: So the Prophet told him to recite, When the earth is shaken with her shaking

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās is credited with saying that al-Zalzalah equals half the Quran because it summarizes Hereafter-related teachings.
rows.anchor: According to a saying attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth’s shaking is a sign of the Hour and belongs to Quranic depictions of the world’s end and human distress.
rows.anchor: The shaking of the earth is considered to be one of the signs of the Hour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth yielding its burdens resembles the earth casting out its contents in 84:3–4.
rows.anchor: This verse is similar to 84:3–4: And when the earth is stretched out, and casts forth what is in it

rows.speaker: a ḥadīth
rows.claim: A report says the earth will expel gold and silver; a murderer, kinship-breaker, and thief will regret their crimes, but nobody will take the treasure.
rows.anchor: A ḥadīth says of this event, “The earth will throw out the pieces of its liver

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Q, Sh
rows.claim: The questioning may be by all people alive then or only disbelievers, since believers already know the world is temporary.
rows.anchor: all human beings who are alive when this event occurs or only to the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth will recount what its inhabitants did on its surface.
rows.anchor: The earth will speak of what its inhabitants did while upon it

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet explains that the earth will testify against each servant, naming deeds and the days they occurred.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said, “Verily, her chronicles means that she will testify against every male and female servant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God inspires or instructs the earth to report every deed of its inhabitants.
rows.anchor: The earth is inspired or instructed to convey all of the deeds performed by those who dwelled upon her

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashtātan can mean people’s divergent final destinies, contrasting those bound for Heaven and Hell.
rows.anchor: implying that people’s ends will diverge greatly and thus alluding to the contrast between those destined for Heaven and those destined for Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively it means people are dispersed like the moths of 101:4; although communities gather in groups, every person is resurrected and judged alone without worldly supports.
rows.anchor: Ashtātan could also be taken to imply that they are dispersed and scattered

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses echo that not even a mote’s weight escapes God’s record.
rows.anchor: Not a mote’s weight evades Him in the heavens or on earth

rows.speaker: Muqātil ibn Sulaymān
rows.claim: Muqātil says the verses address two men: one dismissed tiny gifts to beggars, while the other minimized small sins; both good and evil accumulate.
rows.anchor: According to Muqātil ibn Sulaymān, one of the earliest Quran commentators

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet urged people to fear the Fire even by giving half a date or saying one good word.
rows.anchor: Fear the Fire, even if by giving half a date in charity

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: ʿĀʾishah reports the Prophet warned against sins people belittle because God will account for them.
rows.anchor: The Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah is reported to have said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deeds are recorded in a book or clear book; that record may refer to all deeds or to everything that exists.
rows.anchor: Sometimes this record is understood as a reference to all deeds and at other times as a reference to all that exists

rows.speaker: Bḍ, IK, Ṭs
rows.claim: The witness may be God or the human being: a person may recognize their sins in this life or acknowledge them at Judgment.
rows.anchor: He can be read as a reference to either God or human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators understand ‘good things’ as wealth; it may more broadly mean worldly things loved excessively at the expense of God and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Most commentators equate good things with wealth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All people will be resurrected; graves turning inside out is an apocalyptic inversion that pictures one’s past being raised for judgment.
rows.anchor: All human beings will be resurrected

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: On Resurrection Day good is distinguished from evil and the true nature of actions and hearts becomes known; the Day is when secrets are tested.
rows.anchor: On the Day of Resurrection the good will be clearly distinguished from the bad

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is always aware, but Judgment makes people conscious of that awareness so they can no longer deny their motives or deceive themselves.
rows.anchor: human beings will themselves become cognizant of the fact of God’s ever present awareness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some disbelievers even acknowledge that they deserve Hellfire.
rows.anchor: the disbelievers even bear witness that they deserve Hellfire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qāriʿah comes from a verb meaning to beat or strike with a deafening sound; repeating the question stresses that Judgment is almost impossible to comprehend, so the following verses describe its signs.
rows.anchor: Calamity translates qāriʿah, which comes from the verb qaraʿa

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People will be bewildered and directionless like scattered moths, almost as if drunk, though they will not be drunk.
rows.anchor: human beings will be bewildered, running to and fro with no direction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imagery resembles scattered locusts at resurrection; the present verse likely depicts the end of time, while 54:7 depicts resurrection.
rows.anchor: though 54:7 refers to the Resurrection, while the present verse most likely refers to the end of time

rows.speaker: Āl, Z
rows.claim: Because the Arabic is accusative, an unstated verb is implied, either ‘mention’ or a verb continuing the previous verse, ‘strike.’
rows.anchor: there is an implied word before the sentence, which could be a command to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mountains, firm signs of God, will be moved and scattered on Judgment Day, becoming like shifting sand or wool.
rows.anchor: But on the Day of Judgment, the mountains are set in motion

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: The Fire has reached the greatest possible heat.
rows.anchor: the Fire has reached the greatest heat possible

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: In relation to this Fire, no other fire is truly raging.
rows.anchor: when viewed in relation to this Fire, no other fire is truly raging

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People will know the truth at death; repetition stresses that they cannot escape their actions and will recognize the true worth of what they prized in life.
rows.anchor: This verse means that people will know at the moment of death

rows.speaker: Āl, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: The repeated warning may refer first to punishment in the grave and then to punishment after Resurrection.
rows.anchor: the punishment realized in the grave

rows.speaker: IK, Q
rows.claim: Some say the first warning addresses disbelievers and the second believers.
rows.anchor: the first is addressed to disbelievers and the second to believers

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Kallā may negate or affirm; hence it can be rendered ‘nay’ or ‘indeed’ in either verse.
rows.anchor: The emphatic particle kallā can indicate either negation or affirmation

rows.speaker: IK, Q, Aj
rows.claim: If people knew now what they will know then, competing for more would not distract them; they would turn to God at every moment.
rows.anchor: if people knew now as they will know then, vying for increase (v. 1) would not distract them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional’s answer is omitted for rhetorical force; R supplies either ‘increase would not distract you’ or says it is left vague to make people confront the gravity of their condition.
rows.anchor: The answer to the conditional phrase if you knew is dropped for rhetorical emphasis

rows.speaker: Sh, Ṭ
rows.claim: Knowledge of certainty may mean knowledge of what is certain, namely Resurrection; many also interpret it as the truth of certainty.
rows.anchor: The knowledge of certainty can be interpreted to mean “the knowledge of that which is certain”

rows.speaker: Sufis
rows.claim: Sufis treat knowledge, eye, and truth of certainty as spiritual stages: hearing, seeing or touching, and directly tasting or experiencing.
rows.anchor: Most Sufis see the knowledge of certainty, the eye of certainty (v. 7), and the truth of certainty as three levels of spiritual development

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿArabī
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī distinguishes certainty by indication without obscurity, spiritual witnessing and unveiling, and knowledge of the direct cause; knowing oneself leads from knowledge to sight, then experienced truth.
rows.anchor: the truth of certainty is what is obtained through knowledge of the direct cause

rows.speaker: Āl, Q, Ṭs
rows.claim: Seeing Hellfire may be repeated for emphasis, or refer to seeing it before entry and knowing it with certainty once inside.
rows.anchor: v. 6 can be taken as an indication that people will see Hellfire before entering it

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭs
rows.claim: People are questioned about what they did with God’s earthly blessings, including hearing, sight, and heart.
rows.anchor: People will be questioned about what they have done with the blessings that God bestowed upon them while on earth

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet told companions who had found food after leaving home hungry that they would be questioned about that blessing.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is reported to have said to some of his Companions after they had found food

rows.speaker: Ṭs
rows.claim: Some say people will be asked about the Prophet, considered God’s greatest blessing.
rows.anchor: this verse means people will be questioned about the Prophet, since he is considered the greatest blessing sent by God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning may address only disbelievers or everyone accountable for their actions; it may ask which are the true blessings, worldly delights or those of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: According to some this verse is addressed only to the disbelievers

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: Wayl denotes coming punishment or destruction; some instead take it as the name of a valley in Hell.
rows.anchor: Woe translates wayl, which indicates that punishment or destruction will befall them

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: Mujāhid says humazah harms others with hands and eyes, while lumazah harms them with the tongue.
rows.anchor: According to Mujāhid, humazah, here translated slandering, refers to harm done to others with one’s hands and eyes

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Another view defines humazah as any calumny and lumazah as verbal reproach and accusation.
rows.anchor: humazah indicates any form of calumny, while lumazah indicates verbal reproach and accusation

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Yet another view reverses those meanings and says lumazah literally means eating others’ flesh.
rows.anchor: lumazah literally means to eat the flesh of others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All readings condemn public or private slander and can generally rebuke those more focused on others’ faults than their own.
rows.anchor: all point to the moral decrepitude of those who slander others whether in public or in private

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥuṭamah is a descriptive name for Hell because it crushes everything entering it; the word derives from a verb meaning break, shatter, smash, or crush.
rows.anchor: is one of the descriptive names of Hell

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Afʾidah may mean the heart’s very center, the subtle human faculty that feels pain most severely.
rows.anchor: the very center of the heart, the subtlest faculty of the human being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Fire consumes the core of one’s being and is more painful than any earthly burning.
rows.anchor: the fire touches the very core of one’s being, thus consuming all that one is

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most take these verses to mean Hell’s doors close upon the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: an allusion to the closing of the doors of Hell upon the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muʾṣadah can mean either enclosed or covered.
rows.anchor: which can also mean “covered.”

rows.speaker: Qu
rows.claim: The pillars are pillars of Fire, compared with the enveloping canopies prepared for wrongdoers.
rows.anchor: The pillars are the pillars of the Fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 9 can alternatively be translated ‘as pillars outstretched.’
rows.anchor: V. 9 could also be translated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The early Meccan surah recounts Abrahah’s 570 campaign against the Kaʿbah after he built a church in Sanʿāʾ to divert pilgrims; God repelled his army with birds and stones.
rows.anchor: Abrahah, an Abyssinian general who ruled Yemen, had built a church in Sanʿāʾ

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Many read surahs 105 and 106 together as warning Quraysh that God protected them and the Kaʿbah to prepare for His final Messenger, not because of Quraysh’s status.
rows.anchor: they were not protected because of their status

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: At the conquest of Mecca, the Prophet recalled that God restrained the elephant and restored the sanctuary’s sanctity while granting authority to His Messenger and believers.
rows.anchor: It is said that the Prophet Muhammad invoked the memory of this event during his conquest of Makkah

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Although the verse says one elephant, some reports say Abrahah’s army had eight or twelve.
rows.anchor: some say that Abrahah had eight or twelve elephants with his army

rows.speaker: Ibn Isḥāq
rows.claim: Early histories say the elephant knelt and refused to approach Mecca when beaten, but rose and walked when turned elsewhere.
rows.anchor: the elephant knelt and would not be moved, despite being beaten by the army

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: The wording assumes Arabs know the story and asks why they fail to learn from God’s protection of the Kaʿbah and believe.
rows.anchor: The linguistic structure of the verse indicates that the story was well known to the Arabs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God let Abrahah plan and execute the expedition to his own ruin; this reflects that God is the best of plotters and disbelievers’ plotting goes astray.
rows.anchor: God allowed them to plan the entire expedition and carry it out to their own demise

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Abābīl is understood as groups, successive groups, many birds, or birds coming from every direction.
rows.anchor: interpreted to mean “in groups,” “in successive groups,” “many,” or “coming upon them from every direction”

rows.speaker: most authorities
rows.claim: God sent seabirds such as swallows or herons, each carrying three chickpea- or lentil-sized stones, one in each claw and one in the beak; struck soldiers died, though some lingered on their way to Yemen.
rows.anchor: each carrying three stones the size of chickpeas or lentils, one in each claw and one in the beak

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Some derive sijjīl from Persian words for stone and clay.
rows.anchor: sijjīl, here translated stones of baked clay, is a contraction of two Persian words

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Devoured husks are animal-eaten leaf remains; the surah contrasts Arabia’s greatest army with something among its most insignificant things.
rows.anchor: Devoured husks renders ʿāsfin maʾkūl, which indicates the remains of leaves eaten by animals

rows.speaker: Bg, Z
rows.claim: Several commentators say Ubayy ibn Kaʿb’s Quran manuscript joined al-Fīl and Quraysh as one surah; Ibn Ḥajar takes it as evidence for that reading.
rows.anchor: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb’s manuscript of the Quran had al-Fīl and Quraysh together as one sūrah

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī say ʿUmar recited the two surahs as one in prayer; Ibn Kathīr and others consider them separate despite their semantic connection.
rows.anchor: According to al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī, ʿUmar ibn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first two verses recall Quraysh’s preservation and prosperity, while the last two urge worship because God alone provides and protects.
rows.anchor: The first two verses of this sūrah remind the Quraysh of the blessing they have received

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read as continuation of al-Fīl, the passage can allude to God saving Quraysh from Abrahah’s elephant army.
rows.anchor: Reading this verse as a continuation of the previous sūrah, it can be understood as an allusion to God’s saving the Quraysh from the elephant of Abrahah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Īlāf derives from a root for familiarity or habitual recourse, and later named grants of safe passage to Quraysh from neighboring powers.
rows.anchor: indicating that one is familiar with something or resorts to it habitually

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh traveled to Yemen in winter for Indian spices and goods, then to Syria in summer to sell them and buy agricultural products.
rows.anchor: In the winter the Quraysh would travel to Yemen, where they purchased spices and other commodities coming from India

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Another view is that Kaʿbah custodianship earned Quraysh respect and safe passage, contributing to their wealth.
rows.anchor: the respect the Quraysh received as keepers of the Kaʿbah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘This House’ is the Kaʿbah; Quraysh are urged to recognize that Divine Protection, not their own actions or idols, made them secure.
rows.anchor: This house means the Kaʿbah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage warns of what befalls those who reject Muhammad, as in the town that lost security and provision after denying its messenger; it also recalls Abraham’s prayer.
rows.anchor: these verses allude to the fate that will befall those who reject the Prophet Muhammad

rows.speaker: Muqātil and al-Kalbī
rows.claim: They say the surah was revealed about al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil al-Sahmī.
rows.anchor: Muqātil and al-Kalbī said, “This sūrah was revealed about al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil al-Sahmī”

rows.speaker: Ibn Jurayj
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj says Abū Sufyān struck with a stick an orphan who asked him for something while he was slaughtering his weekly camels, prompting revelation.
rows.anchor: Ibn Jurayj said, “Abū Sufyān was in the habit

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if first tied to one person, the accusation has general force; denying dīn, as religion or Judgment, underlies other sins and violations.
rows.anchor: Even if it was first recorded in reference to a specific individual, it still has a general implication

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn can mean religion or judgment, including denial of Resurrection and the Afterlife.
rows.anchor: Dīn could also mean “judgment” and relate to the denial of the Resurrection and other events of the Afterlife

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Driving away orphans echoes criticism of consuming their inheritances.
rows.anchor: The accusation of driving away the orphan also alludes to the habit of devouring the inheritances of orphans

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse complements the orphan accusation: if verse 2 covers active opposition to moral order, verse 3 covers what one fails to do.
rows.anchor: v. 3 can be seen as a reference to all that one does not do

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternate translation implies the food withheld belongs by right to the indigent, whose acknowledged due is in believers’ wealth.
rows.anchor: implying that the food being withheld from the indigent is actually something to which the indigent have a right

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse admonishes both those who do not feed the poor and those who discourage others, spreading stinginess.
rows.anchor: On the one hand, the present verse admonishes those who do not themselves feed the indigent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those unwilling to feed the needy offer a pseudo-theological excuse by claiming God could feed them if He wished.
rows.anchor: those who do not wish to feed the needy offer a
